theme: How urban trees change neighborhood temperatures

questions.question_set_rationale: Checks a foundational mechanism named in the source.
questions.question_rationale: Asks students to recall the term for water moving through leaves.
questions.question: What process moves water from the soil to the air through tree leaves?
answers: Transpiration
Reflection
Insulation
Condensation
questions.correct_answer_rationale: The passage names transpiration as the movement of water from soil to air through leaves.
questions.comprehension_reference: The student identifies a directly stated scientific term.

questions.question_set_rationale: Checks understanding of the relationship between shade and surface temperature.
questions.question_rationale: Requires explaining the source mechanism rather than recalling a term.
questions.question: Why can a shaded sidewalk release less heat later in the day?
answers: It absorbed less solar energy
It received more rainwater
It became darker in color
It produced more wind
questions.correct_answer_rationale: The source says shaded surfaces absorb less solar energy, stay cooler, and release less heat.
questions.comprehension_reference: The student connects shade, energy absorption, and later heat release.

questions.question_set_rationale: Applies the source’s planning criteria to a new neighborhood scenario.
questions.question_rationale: Students use the stated factors to choose a plausible planting priority.
questions.question: Which location best matches the passage’s approach to prioritizing new trees?
answers: A hot block with little canopy and many heat-vulnerable residents
A cool park with mature trees and low foot traffic
A shaded block selected only because land is inexpensive
A windy plaza where no one lives or waits
questions.correct_answer: A hot block with little canopy and many heat-vulnerable residents
questions.correct_answer_rationale: The passage says planners combine temperature measurements with population-vulnerability information.
questions.comprehension_reference: The student transfers two source criteria to a new case.

questions.question_set_rationale: Analyzes the causal chain connecting canopy shade to neighborhood heat.
questions.question_rationale: Students must order related mechanisms rather than recognize one fact.
questions.question: Which chain best explains how street trees can lower summer heat risk?
answers: More shade → cooler surfaces → less heat released into nearby air
More roots → darker pavement → more heat stored overnight
More leaves → less rainfall → lower afternoon humidity
More branches → taller buildings → stronger winter winds
questions.correct_answer: More shade → cooler surfaces → less heat released into nearby air
questions.correct_answer_rationale: This sequence matches the causal explanation in the first paragraph.
questions.comprehension_reference: The student distinguishes a supported causal chain from plausible-sounding alternatives.

questions.question_set_rationale: Evaluates a proposed heat strategy against the source’s constraints.
questions.question_rationale: Students judge a plan using multiple pieces of evidence.
questions.question: A city proposes planting trees as its only heat-response program. Which evidence from the passage most strongly challenges that plan?
answers: Trees are not a complete solution, and other approaches address needs they cannot
Leaves can block sunlight from pavement
Young trees can grow larger canopies over time
Transpiration moves water through leaves
questions.correct_answer: Trees are not a complete solution, and other approaches address needs they cannot
questions.correct_answer_rationale: The final paragraph explicitly argues for combining trees with several other interventions.
questions.comprehension_reference: The student selects the evidence most relevant to judging the completeness of a policy.

questions.question_set_rationale: Uses the source to design a defensible multi-part heat plan.
questions.question_rationale: The selected response combines mechanisms, implementation constraints, and complementary interventions.
questions.question: Which plan best combines the passage’s ideas into a new neighborhood heat strategy?
answers: Prioritize hot, vulnerable blocks for climate-suitable trees, fund maintenance, and add shade and building improvements
Plant the fastest-growing tree species everywhere and end all other heat programs
Measure temperatures but ignore resident vulnerability and long-term tree care
Build cooling centers only and remove existing street trees to reduce watering
questions.correct_answer: Prioritize hot, vulnerable blocks for climate-suitable trees, fund maintenance, and add shade and building improvements
questions.correct_answer_rationale: This plan integrates targeting, species suitability, maintenance, and multiple interventions from the source.
questions.comprehension_reference: The student combines several source principles into a coherent new plan.
